lessons.title: How LLMs Actually Work (in Plain Words)
lessons.goal: Understand what really happens inside a large language model so you can predict when AI will shine, when it will fail, and how to build systems around its weaknesses.
lessons.audio_intro: Hi, I'm Alex, and welcome to the AI Career track. Before we write a line of code, let's demystify the machine you're building a career on. A large language model is the world's most powerful autocomplete: it reads your message and predicts the likeliest next chunk of text, then the next, and the next. No magic, no database of facts inside. Once you internalize this, everything in this course — hallucinations, context limits, agents, evals — clicks into place. Let's build that intuition now.

sections.body: An LLM generates text one **token** (a word chunk) at a time. Given everything so far, it computes a probability distribution over possible next tokens and picks one — usually a good one, sometimes a lucky one. There is no lookup table of facts and no internal fact-checker. When a model answers your question, it is generating text that *looks like* a good answer, based on patterns absorbed during training. That's why the same model can write brilliant code and confidently invent a fake citation in the same breath. Every professional workflow you'll build in this course exists to catch those moments.

Models are trained in stages. **Pretraining**: the model reads enormous amounts of text and learns to predict the next token — this is where its knowledge of language, code, and the world comes from. **Fine-tuning**: humans rate outputs or provide examples, teaching it to be helpful and follow instructions. **Alignment**: safety and behavior tuning. Practical takeaway: the model's knowledge is frozen at training time, which is why it may not know last month's news unless it has web search, other tools, or you paste the information in. This is exactly why employers pay for engineers who can wire models to live data.

Once you see the model as a pattern-completion engine, its quirks become predictable:

- It **hallucinates** because plausible text, not truth, is its target.
- It **forgets** earlier parts of a long chat because the context window is finite.
- It **follows your format** because it imitates patterns — including your typos.
- It **does better with clear context** — a vague prompt gives the pattern engine too many directions.

Great prompt engineering is really just giving the autocomplete machine an easy pattern to complete. The 2026 agentic stack — tools, retrieval, evals — is engineering wrapped around this one insight.

It is not a search engine, a calculator, or a database — though it can *use* those things when connected to tools, which we build in Module 3. It doesn't 'know' it's right and doesn't have goals. The right mental model: an eager, extremely well-read intern who sometimes bluffs. In 2026, employers don't pay you to chat with that intern — they pay you to deploy it reliably inside software: with retrieval for facts, schemas for structure, and evals for trust. Your job in this track: become the person who ships that. Next lesson, we look at exactly what the job market pays for.

prompts: Explain in one paragraph, like I'm a smart 12-year-old, what happens from the moment I send you a message until I see your answer. Then list 3 things you cannot do because of how you work, and why.
I'm going to describe a task. Tell me whether an LLM alone, an LLM plus tools, or a human is the best fit, and explain in 3 bullet points. Task: [YOUR TASK]

lessons.title: The 2026 AI Job Market Map: Real Titles, Real Demand
lessons.goal: Map the actual 2026 AI job market — agentic hiring stats, real titles like forward-deployed engineer, and the realistic entry path — so you aim this course at jobs that truly exist.
lessons.audio_intro: Alex here. Before you grind through Python and agents, you deserve the map — the honest 2026 picture. Sixty-six percent of AI hiring is now agentic: building AI systems that act, not just chat. The hottest title is 'forward-deployed engineer' — people who ship AI directly into customer environments — hired by Salesforce, Databricks, OpenAI, Palantir, Citi, Cisco, and Anthropic. And only about four percent of AI-engineer postings are entry-level, which is exactly why this course ends with four deployed projects. Let's look at the real terrain.

sections.body: According to the Agentic AI Jobs Index (November 2026), **66% of AI hiring is agentic** — roles about building AI that plans, uses tools, and completes work, not just chatbots. Across 2,584 open agentic roles, the skills employers actually ask for, by share of postings: Python 50%, Cloud 34%, MCP 27%, RAG 26%, Kubernetes 21%, TypeScript 17%, Multi-agent systems 16%, LangChain 15%, LangGraph 13%, Vector databases 13%, Prompt engineering 12%, Tool use 11%, Fine-tuning 10%, Evals 9%. Notice: this course's Modules 2 and 3 teach almost exactly that list, in that order of priority. That's not a coincidence — it's the syllabus the market wrote.

The most in-demand agentic role is the **forward-deployed engineer** — about 18% of agentic demand. It's a hybrid: you understand the customer's workflow, build and adapt agents on site, and ship working software fast. Top employers right now: Salesforce, Databricks, OpenAI, Palantir, Citi, Cisco, and Anthropic. Around it sit related titles you'll actually see on LinkedIn: AI engineer, AI application developer, automation engineer, solutions engineer, agent developer, LLM engineer, data engineer with AI focus. Learn to recognize these — job boards hide gems under inconsistent names, and recruiters search by keyword, not title.

Here's the truth most courses skip: only **~4% of AI-engineer postings are entry-level**. Companies hire juniors as software engineers, data analysts, automation engineers, or AI-application developers — then those people grow into AI roles. So your realistic entry path is: land a role where 'built and shipped an AI feature' is a bonus, then convert. What moves you from the 96% pile to the hired pile is **proof of shipped work**: deployed projects with public links, real users or real data, tested and observable. That's why all four portfolio projects in Module 4 end deployed — a public URL beats a certificate every single time.

Your strategy for the coming weeks:

- **Python first** — it's in 50% of agentic postings, more than everything else combined.
- **Ship, don't study** — Docker, cloud deploys, and a public link are non-negotiable in this course.
- **Target the adjacency** — junior software, data, or automation roles at companies buying agentic AI.
- **Speak the keywords** — RAG, agents, LangGraph, MCP, evals. Recruiters filter by them, and Lesson 17 turns them into your CV.

Keep this lesson handy; we'll return to the numbers when we write your CV and prep interviews.

lessons.title: Context Windows and Why AI Forgets
lessons.goal: Understand tokens and context windows, and learn the professional techniques — summarize, compress, retrieve — that keep long conversations and big documents from falling apart.
lessons.audio_intro: Ever had a chatbot that was brilliant for ten minutes, then suddenly dumb — forgetting your name, your rules, your whole point? That's not the model getting tired; that's the context window doing what it does. Today we go inside the model's short-term memory: tokens, how much a modern model can hold — a lot, but with catches — and the 'lost in the middle' problem. Then the three professional fixes: summarize, compress, retrieve. The third becomes RAG in Lesson 9. This lesson saves you hundreds of frustrating chats.

sections.body: Models don't read words — they read **tokens**, chunks of text roughly three-quarters of a word in English (Hebrew usually costs more tokens per word). The **context window** is everything the model can 'see' at once: your instructions, the conversation history, pasted documents, and its own previous answers. In 2026, windows range from about 128K tokens (roughly a 300-page book) to over a million on some models. Sounds huge — but everything you *add* eats space, every reply accumulates, and long chats die by a thousand crumbs. API pricing is also per token, so wasted context is wasted money.

The catch nobody puts on the marketing page: models are strongest with information at the **beginning and end** of their context, and noticeably weaker with the middle. Stuff 200 pages into a model and ask about page 97, and quality drops — sometimes badly. Bigger windows made 'just paste it all in' *possible*; they did not make it *good*. Professionals treat the context window like a whiteboard: put the important stuff at the top, keep it tidy, and erase what you no longer need. This is also why naive 'chat with your PDF' apps disappoint — the good ones use retrieval, which you'll build yourself in Lesson 9.

**1. Summarize and restart.** When a long chat drifts, ask: *'Summarize our decisions, constraints, and open questions in a compact block.'* Start a fresh chat and paste that block. You keep the knowledge, drop the noise.

**2. Compress with standing instructions.** Keep a short, fixed block — goals, format rules, key facts — at the top of every chat, and reference it instead of re-explaining.

**3. Retrieve instead of remembering.** For large document collections, don't paste everything — fetch only the relevant chunks per question. That's RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), and it's 26% of agentic job postings. You build one from scratch in Lesson 9.

Summarize, compress, retrieve: three words to remember.

sections.h: Context in the code you'll write
sections.body: When you build applications in Module 3, context stops being a chat nuisance and becomes an engineering budget. An agent that appends every tool result to its history will blow the window — and the bill — within a day. Real systems manage context deliberately: trim old messages, summarize completed steps, store full outputs in a database and pass only summaries forward. When you hear terms like 'memory management' or 'context engineering' in job interviews, this is what they mean. You'll implement exactly this pattern in the LangGraph agents of Lesson 11.

prompts: Summarize our conversation so far into a compact handoff block: decisions made, constraints, open questions, and next steps. Keep it under 150 words so I can paste it into a fresh chat.

Here is a long document: [PASTE DOCUMENT]. Give me: (1) a 5-sentence executive summary, (2) a list of the 5 most important facts with where they appear, (3) any contradictions you noticed. Then tell me roughly how many tokens you think it used.
I'm designing an AI app where users upload hundreds of documents. Explain lost-in-the-middle and why I should use retrieval instead of pasting everything, in words a product manager would understand.
lessons.exercise: Take one long, messy chat you've had with an AI this week. Ask the model to summarize it into a handoff block, start a fresh chat with that block, and verify the new chat is as smart as the old one at its best. Write down 2-3 sentences on what you noticed — this is context management, the first real engineering skill of this course.

lessons.title: Hallucinations and How to Catch Them
lessons.goal: Understand why models invent facts, and learn the professional verification techniques — grounding, citations, self-checks, evals — that make AI output trustworthy enough to deploy.
lessons.audio_intro: In 2026, the career-limiting mistake isn't using AI — it's shipping AI output nobody verified. Today, Alex explains why models hallucinate: plausible text, not truth, is what they generate. Then we make it practical: the failure patterns to watch for, verification habits that catch bad output before your boss does, grounding with real sources, and citation checks. And why evals — Lesson 12's quality-control systems — are why companies trust AI at all. Verification separates AI users from AI engineers. Let's get you on the right side.

sections.body: A hallucination is output that is fluent, confident, and wrong. The model isn't lying — it's completing a pattern. When training data was thin or contradictory, the most *plausible* continuation may be invented: a fake API method, a plausible-but-wrong statistic, a citation to a paper that doesn't exist. Classic danger zones: specific numbers, names, dates, quotes, citations, API function signatures, and 'questions where the honest answer is I don't know.' A model asked 'what did the CEO say in the 2024 memo' will often *invent* a quote rather than admit ignorance. Knowing these zones tells you where to point your checks.

The industry-standard answer to hallucination is **grounding**: make the model answer from provided, verified sources rather than memory. Paste the actual memo; retrieve the actual documentation; fetch the live data via a tool. Then instruct: 'Answer ONLY from the provided sources. If the answer is not in them, say so.' Grounded systems are measurably more accurate — and they cite their sources, so a human can verify in seconds. This pattern is RAG (Lesson 9) plus a guardrail, and it's exactly what interviewers mean when they ask 'how do you prevent hallucinations?' Write that answer down now.

sections.h: Catching errors in your own workflow
sections.body:
Habits that catch hallucinations before they ship:

- **Specificity check**: treat every number, name, URL, and citation as guilty until verified. Verify the top three, spot-check the rest.
- **Ask for confidence and citations**: 'List each claim with a confidence level and its source' — then check the sources exist.
- **Adversarial prompt**: 'Critique your own answer above. What might be wrong or unsupported?'
- **Second-model check**: run the output past a different model or a web search.
- **Code is self-verifying**: run it. Tests catch hallucinated APIs instantly — one reason shipped, tested code is your strongest portfolio evidence.

Personal habits don't scale to production. Companies deploy AI behind **evals** — automated test suites for AI output (Lesson 12): golden questions with known answers, LLM-as-judge checks for faithfulness to sources, and observability dashboards that flag suspicious answers. When an employer asks 'how do we trust this agent?', your answer is a pipeline: grounded generation, citations, automated checks, human review for high-stakes answers. That answer is worth salary. For now: every prompt you write in this course should end with a verification step. Make it a reflex.

prompts: Answer this question ONLY from the sources I paste below. After each claim, add [S1], [S2] etc. for the source you used. If the sources don't contain the answer, say 'not in sources.' Question: [QUESTION] Sources: [PASTE SOURCES]
Critique your previous answer like a skeptical senior reviewer: list every claim that is uncertain, unsourced, or possibly fabricated, and rate each as verified / plausible / suspicious.
Here is a list of 5 facts you told me: [LIST]. For each, tell me whether you are confident from training data, guessing, or extrapolating — be brutally honest.
lessons.exercise: Deliberately trigger a hallucination: ask an AI for 'three academic papers about [niche topic] with authors and years.' Then verify each one with web search and record how many were real. Write a 4-sentence reflection on what this means for using AI at work — and keep it; it's a killer interview story about why you build grounded, evaluated systems.

lessons.title: Python Crash Course for AI Work
lessons.goal: Get functionally fluent in the Python you'll actually use for AI engineering — data structures, functions, modules, pip, and the API-and-JSON patterns that dominate real AI codebases.
lessons.audio_intro: Welcome to Module 2. Everything in the 2026 AI job market sits on one language: Python appears in half of all agentic job postings — more than every other skill combined. So today we crash through the Python that matters for AI work. Not theory — the working kind: variables, lists and dictionaries, functions, loops, error handling, and packages. By the end you'll read real AI code without fear and write your first useful script. Already know some Python? Treat this as your diagnostic. Ready? Let's write some code.

sections.h: The 20% of Python that does 80% of AI work
The ecosystem: pip, venv, and reading code
sections.body: Python's superpower is its packages. `pip install requests` and you're talking HTTP; `pip install pydantic` and you have schemas; later, `pip install openai langchain chromadb` and you're building agents. Two rules: always work inside a **virtual environment** (`python -m venv .venv` then activate it) so projects don't poison each other, and pin your dependencies in `requirements.txt`. Learn to *read* package code on GitHub — being able to open a library's source and find what a function really does is a genuine job skill, and it's how you'll debug agent frameworks in Module 3.

Here's the shape of almost every AI script you'll write this course:

```python
import json

def build_prompt(question: str, docs: list[str]) -> str:
    context = "\n".join(f"[{i+1}] {d}" for i, d in enumerate(docs))
    return f"Answer using only these sources:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    docs = ["Refunds take 5 business days.", "VIP users skip the queue."]
    print(json.dumps({"prompt": build_prompt("How long is a refund?", docs)}))
```

Build data in, model call in the middle (Lesson 6), structured data out (Lesson 7). That's the whole profession in one pattern. You'll grow this exact file into your first deployed project.

prompts: I'm learning Python for AI engineering. Give me 10 exercises, increasing difficulty, focused on dicts, lists, functions, error handling, and JSON — the patterns used in LLM application code. No classes, no algorithms.
Here is my Python function: [PASTE CODE]. Review it like a senior engineer: correctness, edge cases, naming, and one concrete improvement. Be specific, not polite.
Explain what this Python code does line by line for a beginner: [PASTE CODE]. Then tell me one bug or bad habit it contains.

Handle empty messages gracefully with try/except. Commit it to the GitHub repo you'll create in Lesson 8 — this is portfolio artifact number one.

lessons.title: Calling LLM APIs from Code (SDKs, Keys, Costs, Retries)
lessons.goal: Call GPT and Claude models from Python like a professional: SDKs, secure API keys, token costs, caching, rate limits, and retry logic that survives the real internet.
lessons.audio_intro: Today you cross the line from AI user to AI builder. We're going to call a frontier model — GPT or Claude — from your own Python code through an API. You'll install the SDK, load your key safely as an environment variable, send your first programmatic request, and read the response like a pro. Then the two things tutorials skip and employers care about: controlling token costs, and retry logic for when the API hiccups. By the end, the engine behind ChatGPT runs on your command. Let's plug in.

sections.body:
An API key turns a chat product into a programmable engine. Get a key from OpenAI or Anthropic, store it as an environment variable (`export OPENAI_API_KEY=...`), and call the model in about five lines:

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_API_KEY automatically
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain RAG in one sentence."}],
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)
```

The same pattern works for Claude (`anthropic` SDK), Gemini, and open models. **Never hardcode keys in code** — keys leaked to GitHub get scraped in minutes. In Lesson 8 you'll add `.env` to `.gitignore` before it bites you.

APIs bill by **token** — roughly a word chunk — with input and output priced separately. A big prompt with a long pasted document can cost more than the answer is worth. Professional cost control: pick the cheapest model that works (mini variants for bulk tasks), cap `max_tokens` on outputs, and **cache**: repeated identical prompts can hit prompt-caching and cost a fraction. Watch your usage dashboard the first week until you internalize the economics. Also know `temperature`: near 0 for deterministic extraction (Lesson 7), higher for creative writing. Choosing model + parameters per task is a real, paid engineering decision — interviewers ask it.

sections.h: From one call to a loop

prompts: I have an OpenAI API key and the Python SDK installed. Walk me through: (1) storing the key safely as an environment variable on my OS, (2) my first chat completion call, (3) printing tokens used and rough cost. Give exact commands.

My script calls an LLM API for 1,000 items and sometimes crashes on rate limits. Give me a robust Python retry pattern with exponential backoff, and explain when to use the SDK's built-in retries instead.

Compare running a task on a frontier model vs a mini model: what factors should I consider for cost, speed, and quality? Give me a decision rule I can apply to batch classification of support tickets.
lessons.exercise: Write `classify_tickets.py`: classify 20 hardcoded support tickets as bug / billing / question using the cheapest sensible model, with retry-with-backoff, per-call token logging, and a final cost summary printed at the end. Store the key in an environment variable. Save the output — it becomes the seed of your Lesson 13 support agent.

lessons.title: Structured Outputs and Schemas (JSON Mode, Pydantic)
lessons.goal: Make LLMs return reliable, validated JSON with schemas and Pydantic — the single technique that turns a chatbot into a component real software can trust.
lessons.audio_intro: Here's a secret about production AI: almost nothing uses free text. Every serious AI feature you've used is the model filling in a form — a JSON object with exact fields — so a website, database, or agent can actually do something with the answer. Today you'll learn structured outputs: JSON mode, response formats, and Pydantic validation. This is where AI stops being a demo and starts being software. It's also a favorite interview question: 'how do you guarantee valid JSON?' By the end, you'll answer it with code.

sections.body: If a model answers 'Sure! The category is probably billing, I think 😊' — a human shrugs, a program crashes. Downstream code needs predictable structure: `{"category": "billing", "confidence": 0.9}`. Structured output means constraining the model to emit **valid JSON matching a schema**, every time. The provider-level tricks: **JSON mode** (forces syntactically valid JSON) and newer **schema-constrained outputs**, where you pass the exact shape and the API guarantees it. Combined with Pydantic on your side, you get a contract: if the model deviates, your code catches it — instead of your users catching it.

sections.h: Pydantic: your schema is your validator
sections.body:
Pydantic lets you define the shape once and reuse it for prompting and validation:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Ticket(BaseModel):
    category: str = Field(..., description="one of: bug, billing, question")
    urgency: int = Field(..., ge=1, le=5)
    summary: str = Field(..., max_length=120)

resp = client.beta.chat.completions.parse(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ticket_text}],
    response_format=Ticket,
)
ticket = resp.choices[0].message.parsed  # a real Ticket object
```

If the model returns garbage, Pydantic raises `ValidationError` — and you retry (Lesson 6). LangChain, FastAPI, and half the 2026 AI stack speak Pydantic natively. Learn it once, use it everywhere.

Production pattern, memorize it:

1. Define the schema (Pydantic).
2. Call the model with `response_format=YourSchema`.
3. Validate the parse; on failure, **retry with the error message** — models self-correct well: 'Your last output failed validation: urgency must be 1-5. Return corrected JSON only.'
4. Cap retries (2–3); then fall back (queue for human review, return `None`, or use a default).

This loop — schema, call, validate, retry-with-error — is the backbone of the agents you build in Lessons 11–16. It's also most of what 'LLM application engineering' means in job descriptions. Write it as a reusable function once; import it forever.

Scales of structure: an `enum` for classification ('bug'/'billing'/'question' — nothing else can come back), a list of nested objects for extraction (every invoice line with amount and date), and unions for routing (this request is a Refund or a Complaint). Practical rules that keep accuracy high: keep schemas **flat and small** — every field is another chance to err; give each field a clear `description` the model reads as instructions; and prefer many small structured calls over one mega-schema. You'll reuse exactly these schemas in RAG (Lesson 9) and the support agent (Lesson 13).

prompts: Here is my Pydantic model: [PASTE CODE]. Generate 5 diverse test inputs for it and the exact JSON each should produce, so I can unit-test my extraction pipeline.

My LLM sometimes returns invalid JSON despite JSON mode: trailing commas, unescaped quotes, markdown fences. Give me a robust Python `safe_parse` function that handles the common failure modes and retries once with the error fed back to the model.

Design a Pydantic schema for extracting structured data from customer support emails: category, urgency 1-5, entities mentioned, suggested reply. Include field descriptions that work as model instructions.
lessons.exercise: Extend Lesson 6's ticket classifier: replace free-text classification with a Pydantic `Ticket` schema, use structured output mode, and add the validate-retry loop with a max of 3 attempts. Write 3 unit tests with fake responses (one valid, one invalid, one rate-limited) proving the loop behaves. Push to GitHub — tested structured-output code is exactly what AI-application job posts ask for.

lessons.title: Git & GitHub Essentials for AI Engineers
lessons.goal: Master the daily Git workflow — commits, branches, pull requests — and set up a GitHub profile that recruiters can actually read, so your code becomes career evidence.
lessons.audio_intro: Quick question: how will a recruiter know you can code? Not from a certificate — from your GitHub. In this lesson we cover the professional Git workflow — repos, commits, branches, pull requests — plus the habits that make your work legible: small commits, clear messages, a clean README. Git is also how every AI team collaborates, on code, prompts, and evals alike. And there's a security angle: we'll make sure your API keys never get committed. A short lesson with an oversized career payoff. Let's commit.

sections.body:
Git is a time machine for code; GitHub is where the timeline lives publicly. The professional loop:

```bash
git init && git add . && git commit -m "first ticket classifier"
git branch feature/streaming
git switch feature/streaming
# ...work, then: git add -p && git commit -m "add streaming"
git push -u origin feature/streaming  # then open a PR
```

Commit small and often, with messages that say *why* ('retry on 429 to survive rate limits') not what. Branch per feature. Open a pull request even on your own repos — it documents your thinking and proves you know the team workflow employers assume. If your history is one giant 'final version' commit, you look like an amateur. If it's clean, you look hireable.

The fastest way to burn money as a beginner: commit an API key. Bots scrape GitHub for leaked keys within minutes of a push. Defenses, in order:

1. `.gitignore` containing `.env`, `.venv/`, `__pycache__/` — create it **before** the first commit.
2. Keep keys in `.env`, load with `python-dotenv`.
3. Rotate any key that ever touched a commit — assume it's compromised.
4. Run a secret scanner (e.g. `gitleaks`) before pushing; GitHub flags leaks automatically, but rotation is still your job.

This is a real interview filter question ('how do you handle secrets?') and a real production responsibility. Get it right from repo number one.

A repo with no README is a locked shop. Every project repo you make in this course gets: a one-line description ('Support-ticket agent that classifies, retrieves, and answers — deployed'), a 30-second quickstart (`pip install -r requirements.txt`, `cp .env.example .env`, `docker compose up`), a screenshot or short demo GIF, an architecture note ('FastAPI → LangGraph agent → pgvector'), and a link to the live deployment. The README is what a recruiter sees in 15 seconds — the code is what an engineer sees at minute five. Both matter; Lesson 20 polishes this into a portfolio. Start the habit now.

AI repos have extra versioned artifacts: prompts, eval datasets, eval results, and deployment configs. Professionals commit prompt files as code (`prompts/classify_v3.txt`), version eval sets alongside the code that scores them, and record in the commit message which model and settings produced which score ('gpt-4o-mini, temp 0, 91% on eval v3 — up from 87%'). That traceability is what lets a team trust a prompt change. When your Lesson 12 evals run in CI on every push — yes, you'll do that — your repos become self-proving: code, prompts, and quality evidence in one public place.

prompts: Review my last 10 git commit messages and rewrite them as a senior engineer would: [PASTE MESSAGES]. Explain the pattern you applied.

Create a complete .gitignore for a Python AI project that uses .env files, a virtualenv, chromadb/pgvector data dirs, and Jupyter. Then list the 5 most common beginner git mistakes and the fix for each.

Write a README template for an AI project repo with: hook line, demo link, quickstart, architecture diagram description, eval results table, and tech-stack badges. Fill it with realistic example content for a RAG support agent.

Confirm your API key is NOT in the history (`gitleaks detect` or search the repo for the key). This repo is your Module 4 foundation — everything ships here.

lessons.title: RAG from Scratch: Chunking, Embeddings, Vector DB
lessons.goal: Build retrieval-augmented generation from first principles — chunking, embeddings, vector search, and grounded answering — the skill behind 26% of agentic job postings.
lessons.audio_intro: Welcome to Module 3 — the engine room of your career. Today, RAG: retrieval-augmented generation, the technique that lets an AI answer from your documents instead of its training data. It's in twenty-six percent of agentic job postings and powers 'chat with your data' products everywhere. We'll build it from scratch: split documents into chunks, turn text into embeddings — numbers that capture meaning — store them in a vector database, and search by similarity. No frameworks today, just Python. Build RAG bare, and every wrapper becomes trivial. Let's retrieve.

sections.body: Two problems, one solution. Models don't know your private data, and context windows choke on whole archives. RAG fixes both: at **index time**, split documents into chunks, convert each to an **embedding** (a vector of numbers where similar meanings sit close together), and store them in a **vector database**. At **query time**, embed the user's question, find the nearest chunks, and paste only those into the prompt as context. The model now answers from fresh, specific, *citable* sources — hallucinations drop, and you can show exactly which paragraph produced the answer. That's the whole idea; everything else is engineering.

Chunk size decides RAG quality. Too small: you retrieve fragments without context. Too big: noise dilutes the signal and costs tokens. Start around 300–500 tokens with 10–15% overlap, and — the pro move — chunk on structure: headers, paragraphs, or sections, not arbitrary character counts. A basic splitter:

```python
def chunk(text: str, size: int = 400, overlap: int = 50) -> list[str]:
    words = text.split()
    return [" ".join(words[i:i+size])
            for i in range(0, len(words), size - overlap)]
```

Always attach metadata — source file, heading, page — or your answers can't cite. Interview classic: 'how would you chunk a 200-page PDF with tables?' Have an opinion.

An embedding model maps text to a point in space where meaning = distance: 'refund policy' lands near 'money-back guarantee', far from 'kubernetes'. OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small` or open alternatives both work fine. Store vectors in a vector DB — Chroma for local dev, pgvector for Postgres shops, Pinecone for managed scale:

```python
import chromadb

db = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./rag_data")
col = db.get_or_create_collection("docs")
col.add(documents=chunks, ids=[str(i) for i in range(len(chunks))])
hits = col.query(query_texts=[question], n_results=4)
```

Top-k similarity search (k=3–5) returns the chunks you paste into the prompt. Vector DBs are in 13% of agentic postings — this is that skill.

The final pattern, combining everything from Modules 2 and 3:

```python
context = "\n\n".join(
    f"[S{i+1}] {c}" for i, c in enumerate(hits["documents"][0])
)
prompt = (f"Answer ONLY from the sources. Cite [S#] after each claim. "
          f"Say 'not in sources' if absent.\n\n{context}\n\nQ: {question}")
```

Then the discipline that separates pros from demo-builders: test it. Keep 20 golden questions with known answers; when you change chunk size, model, or top-k, re-run and compare (Lesson 12 makes this automated). Bad retrieval is silent — only evals catch it. Next lesson we wrap this engine in an API and ship it to the internet.

lessons.title: Shipping a RAG Endpoint (FastAPI + Docker Intro)
lessons.goal: Wrap your RAG engine in a FastAPI endpoint, containerize it with Docker, and deploy it to a public URL — the moment your portfolio becomes a link anyone can click.
lessons.audio_intro: Today is a milestone. Everything so far ran on your laptop; today we ship it to the internet. We'll wrap your RAG engine in FastAPI — Python's standard API framework — define clean requests and responses, then containerize it with Docker so it runs identically everywhere. Then we deploy it and get a real public URL. Why does this matter? Because 'I built a RAG' is a claim, but 'here's the link, try it' is proof — and cloud skills sit in a third of agentic postings. Let's go live.

sections.body:
FastAPI turns a function into a URL:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str

class Answer(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    sources: list[str]

@app.post("/ask", response_model=Answer)
def ask(body: Ask) -> Answer:
    hits = retrieve(body.question)
    return Answer(answer=generate(body.question, hits),
                  sources=[h["id"] for h in hits])
```

Pydantic (Lesson 7) validates both directions automatically, and `/docs` gives you a live test page for free. Load the index at startup, not per request, and add a `/health` endpoint — deploy platforms ping it. This is the exact shape of every AI microservice you'll build in Module 4.

'Works on my machine' is not a deployment. Docker packs your app + Python + dependencies into one image that runs identically on your laptop, a cloud VM, or a Kubernetes pod (that last one is 21% of agentic postings — this lesson is your doorway). The whole file:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

Build with `docker build -t rag-api .`, run with `docker run -p 8000:8000 rag-api`. One command, and your environment is reproducible forever. List `docker` on your CV only after this works — then list it proudly.

sections.h: Deploy it: a URL anyone can click
sections.body: Free and near-free tiers make shipping painless in 2026: Railway, Render, Fly.io, Hugging Face Spaces, or a small cloud VM — pick one and learn it. The universal checklist: set your API key as a **platform environment variable** (never in the image), include a `/health` route, and keep a persistent disk (or re-embed at startup) for your vector index. After deploy, your README gets its most important line: `Live demo: https://your-app.example.com/docs`. Every Module 4 project repeats this loop, so invest an extra hour now to make it smooth — deployment fluency is a compounding skill, and 'deployed' is the word that separates your portfolio from every course graduate who only has localhost.

sections.h: Basic CI: tests on every push
sections.body:
One small GitHub Actions file and your repo starts proving itself:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: {python-version: "3.12"}
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest
```

Now every push runs your unit tests (you wrote them in Lesson 7), and a green checkmark appears on your repo. Recruiters may not read the YAML, but engineers do — and 'CI/CD' on your CV now has a public, clickable receipt. Lesson 12 adds your eval suite to this same pipeline.

lessons.title: Agents with LangChain, LangGraph, Function Calling, and MCP
lessons.goal: Build real agents — LLMs that decide, call tools, and recover — using function calling, LangGraph state machines, and the Model Context Protocol; the core skills of the 2026 agentic job market.
lessons.audio_intro: This is the lesson the whole market points at. Sixty-six percent of AI hiring is agentic, and today you build a real agent: an LLM that doesn't just answer — it decides what to do, calls tools, checks results, and tries again when things break. We'll start with function calling, the raw primitive. Then LangGraph, in thirteen percent of postings, for multi-step control. And finally MCP — the Model Context Protocol — the 2026 standard for tools, at twenty-seven percent. The heart of your career. Let's build.

sections.h: Function calling: the atom of agency

sections.body:
A naive agent loop spirals: infinite retries, lost context, unbounded cost. **LangGraph** (in 13% of agentic postings) models the agent as a **graph** — nodes are steps (call model, run tool, human check), edges are transitions, and a state object carries the data. Key disciplines: conditional edges (route on the model's tool choice), a recursion limit (hard cap on steps), and checkpoints (persist state so a long agent survives restarts and can be replayed):

```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph

g = StateGraph(AgentState)
g.add_node("model", call_model)
g.add_node("tools", run_tools)
g.set_entry_point("model")
g.add_conditional_edges("model", route, {"tools": "tools", "end": END})
app = g.compile()
```

LangChain (15% of postings) supplies the surrounding ecosystem — model wrappers, retrievers, prompts. You'll use both; understand the graph underneath.

sections.h: Designing agents that don't embarrass you
sections.body:
The difference between a demo and a system:

- **Small tool sets** — 3–6 sharp tools beat 30 vague ones; models confuse themselves with too many.
- **Good descriptions** — tool docs are prompts; 'Fetch CURRENT order status from the orders DB, not history' saves hours.
- **Hard limits** — recursion cap, token budget, timeout. Agents must be able to *stop*.
- **Tracing** — log every step (model call, tool, result); Lesson 12 makes it observable.
- **Human gates for irreversible actions** — refunds, deletes, emails get a confirmation node.

Next lesson: how we prove these agents actually work — evals and observability, the 9% skill that everything else depends on.

prompts: I'm designing an agent that must [TASK: e.g. research a topic and write a report]. Give me: a node-by-node LangGraph design, the tool set with exact names/descriptions/parameters, where to place human gates, and failure modes to guard.

Explain MCP (Model Context Protocol) like I'm a senior engineer who knows function calling: what problem it solves vs plain tool use, client vs server roles, and when I'd write my own MCP server instead of inline tools.
My agent loops forever / burns tokens / picks wrong tools. Give me a prioritized debugging checklist covering prompts, tool descriptions, graph structure, and limits — with one concrete fix each.
lessons.exercise: Build `research_agent.py`: a LangGraph agent with 3 real tools (web search, a notes store, and your Lesson 10 RAG's `/ask` endpoint via HTTP), a recursion limit of 8 steps, and full step logging. Then wrap one of the tools as an MCP server too. Give it a real research task and save the trace. Push both to GitHub — 'LangGraph agent + MCP server' covers three of the top-ten agentic skills in one repo.

lessons.title: Evals and Observability: LLM-as-Judge Basics
lessons.goal: Prove your AI works — with test sets, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and tracing — the quality-control skill that turns 'it seems good' into 'it measurably improved, and here's the graph.'
lessons.audio_intro: The most underrated skill in AI hiring: evals. Nine percent of agentic postings ask for it, but one hundred percent of serious teams depend on it, because every stakeholder asks the same question: 'how do we know it works?' Today you'll build an evaluation suite — a golden dataset with known answers, automated scoring including an LLM-as-judge, and traces showing exactly what your agent did and where it went wrong. Evals are why teams can change a prompt on Friday and sleep on the weekend. Let's measure.

sections.h: Why 'it seems fine' isn't a quality bar
sections.body: You change a prompt; three manual tests look okay; you ship; accuracy quietly drops 12%. Without evals, AI quality is invisible until users complain — or until your demo fails in front of a stakeholder. An **eval suite** is a fixed dataset plus automated scoring, run on every change. Three levels: **unit checks** (did it return valid JSON? did it cite sources?), **golden-set scoring** (accuracy on N known questions), and **model-graded evals** (an LLM judging open-ended output). The habit to build now: every project in Module 4 ships with its eval results in the README — a table of scores recruiters and interviewers can see.

Golden set: 20–50 real questions with known-good answers. Runner: same code path as production, offline scoring:

```python
def run_evals(cases, answer_fn, judge):
    results = []
    for c in cases:
        out = answer_fn(c["question"])
        score = judge(c["question"], out, c["expected"])
        results.append({"id": c["id"], "score": score})
    passed = sum(r["score"] >= 4 for r in results)
    return {"pass_rate": passed / len(results), "results": results}
```

Store results as JSON per run, tagged with model + prompt version — this is your regression baseline. When you tune chunk size or prompts in the projects, you *re-run this* and show the delta. 'I improved RAG answer accuracy from 71% to 88% with these changes' is a resume bullet with receipts.

Open-ended output can't be string-matched, so a stronger model grades it against a rubric: 'Score 1–5: is the answer faithful to the sources? Penalize unsupported claims.' Rules that make judges reliable: a **fixed rubric** with explicit criteria; **faithfulness first** ('grounded in provided context, not general knowledge'); **show the judge the sources**; and **calibrate on a human-labeled sample** — run 10 cases graded by you and by the judge, compare, and adjust the rubric until they agree. Use a stronger model for judging than for generating. A good judge is itself a structured-output problem — Lesson 7 returns. Bias traps (verbosity, self-preference) exist; your calibration step is the defense.

Evals score the outcome; **traces** show the journey: every model call, tool invocation, latency, token count, and error, per request. Lightweight start — structured logging:

```python
import logging, time, json
log = logging.getLogger("agent")

t0 = time.time()
log.info("event=tool_call name=get_order id=%s", order_id)
# ... later ...
log.info("event=answer latency=%.2fs tokens=%d", time.time()-t0, n)
```

That's real observability in embryo — production teams graduate to platforms like LangSmith or OpenTelemetry, same concepts, nicer UIs. Wire your Lesson 11 agent's traces into an eval run and you can answer the interview classic: 'your agent's accuracy dropped this week — walk me through debugging it.' You'll have literally done it.

prompts: Design an eval suite for my [PROJECT: e.g. support agent with RAG]: golden-set categories, 15 example questions with expected behaviors, unit checks, and an LLM-as-judge rubric. Output as a table plus the rubric text.
Here are 5 real outputs from my agent with their sources: [PASTE]. As a strict judge, score each 1-5 for faithfulness and cite any unsupported claim. Then summarize the failure pattern.
My eval pass rate dropped from 88% to 74% after I changed [PROMPT/MODEL/CHUNKING]. Give me a systematic debugging procedure using traces and per-category eval breakdown to isolate the cause.
lessons.exercise: Build `evals/` for your Lesson 10 RAG endpoint: a 20-question golden set (JSON), a runner script that calls the endpoint, an LLM-as-judge with a written rubric, results saved per run, and add it to your GitHub Actions CI. Put the pass rate in the README with the date. You now have the full professional loop: deployed system + automated proof it works. Module 4 builds on exactly this.

lessons.title: Project 1: Customer-Support Agent (LangGraph, Deployed)
lessons.goal: Build and deploy a complete customer-support agent with LangGraph — classification, RAG over FAQ docs, safe tool actions, human gate for refunds — your first portfolio-grade shipped project.
lessons.audio_intro: Welcome to Module 4 — where your career actually gets built. Only about four percent of AI-engineer postings are entry-level, so your ticket in is shipped proof. Project one is the most requested AI feature in business: a customer-support agent. A customer asks anything; it classifies intent, retrieves the answer from a knowledge base, and takes safe actions like order lookup — with a human gate before anything irreversible. LangGraph, Docker, and a public URL employers can click. Lessons one through twelve become one system. Let's build it.

sections.body:
One repo, one agent, four components you already know:

1. **Classifier** — structured output (Lesson 7): route each message to `faq`, `order_status`, or `refund`.
2. **RAG node** — your Lesson 9 engine over a real FAQ/knowledge base.
3. **Tools** — `get_order_status`, `create_refund` (function calling, Lesson 11).
4. **Human gate** — refunds above a threshold pause for confirmation; everything else flows.

In LangGraph terms: a classifier node with conditional edges to three branches, tool nodes, and a confirm node. This is a `StateGraph` with a recursion limit and checkpointer — you wrote that skeleton in Lesson 11. Now it does something a business would pay for: deflect tier-one support tickets with citations, and escalate the rest.

Build the boring way, test each layer before adding the next:

1. Data first: 30–50 real FAQ entries (use a public support docs page, or your own company's). Chunk, embed, load Chroma at startup.
2. Classifier with Pydantic schema — unit-test with 15 hardcoded messages (include typo'd and angry ones).
3. RAG node with `[S#]` citations and 'not in sources' behavior.
4. Tool nodes with mocked order data; log every call.
5. The refund gate: `pending_refunds` in state, a `/confirm` endpoint, and a message to a human channel (even just a log line for the demo).

Each step is small and provable — that's how professionals de-risk a build, and how your git history tells a story an engineer will respect.

Deployment repeats the Lesson 10 loop: FastAPI app, `/chat` and `/health` endpoints, Dockerfile, free-tier deploy, CI on push. What makes this portfolio-grade rather than a course exercise:

- **Evals in CI** (Lesson 12): a 30-case golden set — routing accuracy, answer faithfulness, refund-gate correctness — with the pass rate in the README.
- **A demo script**: 3 example conversations in the README showing escalation, RAG citation, and the human gate.
- **A trace sample**: one logged agent run, pretty-printed — proof you can debug what you ship.
- **Cost note**: 'gpt-4o-mini, ~$0.002 per ticket' — engineering judgment on display.

README, code, live link, eval table: that's the full professional package.

This project maps directly onto the 2026 market: LangGraph (13% of agentic postings), RAG (26%), tool use (11%), evals (9%), Docker + cloud (34%). In interviews it becomes your anchor story: 'I built a support agent with a classification-to-action pipeline, grounded answers with citations, a human gate on refunds, and an eval suite in CI — deployed, here's the link.' Structure it as situation → design choices → one real bug you traced with logs → eval numbers before/after a fix. Next lesson: project two, document intelligence with RAG — the same engine pointed at higher-value data.

Write 30 realistic customer messages for a support agent golden set: 10 FAQ, 10 order-status, 10 refund — include angry, typo'd, ambiguous, and out-of-scope cases, labeled with expected route and behavior.

Post the link where one real person can try it (a community, a friend's Slack). Log what broke and fix it. This is portfolio artifact one of four — make it count.

lessons.title: Project 2: Document Analyzer with RAG
lessons.goal: Build a document-intelligence app — upload documents, extract structured fields, ask grounded questions with page-level citations — and deploy it publicly.
lessons.audio_intro: Project two attacks the most common enterprise AI use case of 2026: document intelligence. Companies sit on contracts, invoices, reports, and PDFs — and pay well for tools that read them. You'll build a document analyzer: upload documents, the system chunks and embeds them, extracts structured fields with schemas, and answers questions with page-level citations. Same RAG engine as project one, but multi-document, with extraction — so it feels like a product. Deployed, with a live demo over a public PDF. 'Chat with your documents' becomes your code. Let's build.

sections.body: Support agents deflect tickets; document analyzers save professional hours — reviewing a contract, auditing invoices, summarizing reports. That's budget-line value, which is why 'document AI' and 'intelligent document processing' appear in a huge slice of real postings. Your version: a user uploads PDFs or text files; the app parses them, chunks **on structure** (pages, sections, tables — your Lesson 9 chunking opinions finally matter), embeds into a per-user collection, and offers two modes: **Q&A** with `[page N]` citations, and **extraction** into Pydantic schemas (e.g. from an invoice: vendor, amounts, dates, line items). Same primitives, productized.

Architecture in one flow:

```
upload → parse (pypdf) → chunk + metadata(page, section)
      → embed → Chroma collection per document
Q&A:   question → retrieve top-5 → grounded answer + citations
Extract: schema + retrieve relevant chunks → Pydantic-validated fields
```

Two details that separate you from every 'chat with PDF' demo:

1. **Citations are clickable**: the answer links to the retrieved chunk and its page number, displayed in the UI. Verifiability is the product.
2. **Extraction is validated**: extraction is a per-field confidence score — and low-confidence fields are flagged, not silently guessed.

That's grounded, verifiable, production-shaped thinking — exactly what an AI-application interview probes for.

A document tool with no documents is a car with no gas. Ship it with: two pre-loaded public sample documents (a real open-source license agreement, a sample invoice), a drag-and-drop upload box, and a side panel showing retrieved chunks for every answer. Keep the stack honest and clean: FastAPI + your RAG engine + a single-page frontend (plain HTML/JS or Streamlit — the point is the pipeline, not the pixels). Reuse Lesson 10's Docker and deploy loop. Evals: a 20-question golden set on the sample docs with expected citations — faithfulness scored by your Lesson 12 judge. README shows the eval table next to the demo link.

Small touches that make engineers and hiring managers nod: **per-document collections** deleted when a user removes the doc (data hygiene); a **file-type and size guard** with clear errors; **scan-friendly text extraction** with a fallback note when a PDF is image-only; and a **cost readout** (tokens per question, roughly in dollars). None of these are hard; all of them are what 'production mindset' means concretely. In your README, write one paragraph titled 'what I'd do at 10x scale': batch embedding, a job queue, pgvector, per-tenant isolation. That paragraph is a conversation starter in every interview — it shows you see past the demo.

prompts: Design a Pydantic extraction schema for [DOCUMENT TYPE: invoice / contract / lab report] with per-field descriptions that double as model instructions. Include confidence and a required source-page reference per field.

My document analyzer retrieves the wrong chunks for table-heavy PDFs. Give me a prioritized improvement plan: parsing, chunking strategy, table handling, query rewriting, hybrid search. One experiment per item.

Write the 'what I'd do at 10x scale' section of my README: assume 10k documents and 100 concurrent users. Cover storage, embedding jobs, queues, cost, and per-tenant isolation — in confident, concrete engineer voice.

In the README, include the '10x scale' section. Portfolio artifact two is done — and your RAG story now has two deployed variants, which is exactly what RAG's 26% of job postings wants to see.

lessons.title: Project 3: Multi-Agent Content Pipeline
lessons.goal: Build a multi-agent content pipeline — researcher, writer, and editor agents coordinating through a LangGraph graph — and deploy it as a working product with evals.
lessons.audio_intro: Project three: multi-agent systems — sixteen percent of agentic job postings ask for it by name. Instead of one overloaded agent, a team of specialists with narrow tools and clear jobs, coordinated by a graph. You'll build a content pipeline: a researcher agent that gathers and cites sources, a writer agent that drafts only from those sources, and an editor agent that scores the draft against a rubric and sends it back for revision. Traces mandatory, revision cap non-negotiable. This proves you can orchestrate complexity. Let's assemble the team.

sections.body:
One agent with 20 tools and one giant prompt confuses itself — the failure you met in Lesson 11. The multi-agent answer: **decompose**. Each agent gets a small toolset, a focused prompt, and one job:

- **Researcher**: search + retrieve, output = a sourced brief (claims with links).
- **Writer**: draft from the brief ONLY — no new facts allowed, by prompt contract.
- **Editor**: LLM-as-judge rubric (accuracy-to-brief, tone, structure, length) with a 1–5 score per criterion; below threshold, send back with the critique attached.

In LangGraph: three node-pairs (model + tools each), a shared `PipelineState` carrying the brief, draft, scores, and revision count, and a conditional loop editor → writer capped at 2 revisions. The cap is not optional — it's what makes the graph terminate.

Multi-agent systems live and die on their **interfaces**. Define them as Pydantic models before writing any prompts:

```python
class Source(BaseModel):
    claim: str
    url: str

class Brief(BaseModel):
    topic: str
    sources: list[Source]

class Draft(BaseModel):
    content_markdown: str
    citations: list[str]

class Critique(BaseModel):
    scores: dict[str, int]   # accuracy, tone, structure
    verdict: Literal["approve", "revise"]
    notes: str
```

Because agents pass validated objects — not free text — a bad writer output fails at the schema, not in the reader's hands. This is Lesson 7 scaled up to system design, and it's the single best answer to the interview question 'what's hard about multi-agent systems?' Contracts.

When a three-agent pipeline produces a mediocre result, 'which agent failed?' must be answerable in one minute. Log every hop: the brief (with sources), each draft, each critique with scores, token counts per agent, and total wall time. Surface it in the UI — a collapsible 'pipeline trace' panel. This transforms the product from a magic box into an inspectable system, and it's precisely how real agent platforms (LangGraph-based ones included) sell themselves. Your eval suite: end-to-end — run 5 topics, editor-score the outputs, assert revision counts stay under the cap, and track total cost per run. Cost per run in the README is a beautiful, senior-sounding number.

Deploy like the others (FastAPI + Docker + free tier, public URL), with a queue — pipeline runs take a minute, so submit a topic, get a job ID, poll for the result. Demo mode: two pre-run example topics so the link never shows an empty screen. Position it in the README as what it is: 'a LangGraph multi-agent pipeline with typed agent contracts, an evaluator loop, and full traces.' That sentence hits multi-agent (16%), LangGraph (13%), evals (9%), and observability in one line. Then write the blog-post version — a short 'how I built it' (Lesson 20 turns it into LinkedIn gold). Next lesson: your capstone — a personal-assistant agent that ties the whole course together.

My multi-agent pipeline outputs drafts with facts not in the research brief. Give me 5 root-cause hypotheses ranked by likelihood, and a concrete test for each (prompt contract, schema enforcement, trace inspection).

lessons.title: Project 4 + Capstone: Personal-Assistant Agent with Tool Use
lessons.goal: Build your capstone — a personal-assistant agent with MCP tools, memory, and a web UI — deployed, evaluated, and packaged as the centerpiece of your portfolio and your course certificate.
lessons.audio_intro: The capstone. Everything this course taught you, in one product: a personal-assistant agent. It chats naturally, remembers facts about you across sessions, manages to-dos and calendar through real tools, answers questions with web search and sources — and, the 2026 flourish, exposes its tools as an MCP server so other agents can drive it too. Fully deployed with a public URL, wrapped in evals, documented like a real product. This is the project you lead interviews with, and your final submission for the BINA certificate. One system, everything you know.

sections.body:
Your assistant does five things, each mapping to a skill from the market index:

1. **Natural conversation** — a LangGraph agent with a short system persona and a recursion limit.
2. **Memory** — long-term facts (name, preferences, projects) stored outside the context window: extract with a structured-output step, store in SQLite, inject a compact summary into each session. This is Lesson 3's 'summarize, compress, retrieve' as engineering.
3. **Task tools** — add/complete/list to-dos and calendar events (function calling).
4. **Web answer tool** — search + fetch, with sources in every answer.
5. **MCP exposure** — the task tools also served via an MCP server, so Claude or any MCP client can drive your assistant.

Docker + deploy + evals + README: the full Lesson 13–15 treatment, with a real UI and a memory demo you can show in 30 seconds.

Memory is where beginners show and engineers shine. Design:

```python
class Memory(BaseModel):
    facts: list[Fact]  # {key, value, confidence, updated_at}

async def remember(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    extracted = await extract_facts(state.messages)   # structured output
    upsert(db, extracted)                            # SQLite
    state.system_extra = compact_summary(db)         # ≤150 tokens
    return state
```

Run `remember` at session end, inject the compact summary at session start. Two rules keep it sane: memory is **extracted, not raw** (store 'prefers short answers', not the whole chat) and **bounded** (a summary under 150 tokens, or you've rebuilt the context-window problem). 'How would you add memory to an agent?' is a standard interview question — you'll answer with code you shipped.

The capstone eval suite is your certificate's technical core:

- **Memory tests**: tell it a fact in session 1, assert it's recalled in session 2 (5 scripted cases).
- **Tool tests**: unit-test each tool; integration-test the routing ('remind me tomorrow at 9' → calendar tool, not chat).
- **Web-answer faithfulness**: 10 questions scored by your LLM-as-judge for source-grounding.
- **Safety**: one test where the user asks for a destructive action and the agent confirms first.

All in CI, results in the README, with a **demo script** that walks a viewer through conversation → memory recall → tool use → MCP connection in under three minutes. Record that walkthrough as your demo video. Practice it until smooth; in Module 6 you'll perform a version of it live.

Final submission for the BINA certificate (exam in Lesson 24): repo link, deployed URL, demo video, README with architecture diagram, eval table, and a one-page 'design decisions' doc covering what you chose, what you rejected, and why. Then re-pin all four portfolio repos at the top of your GitHub profile — support agent, document analyzer, multi-agent pipeline, personal assistant. That's four deployed systems covering Python, RAG, LangGraph, LangChain, MCP, vector DBs, evals, Docker, and cloud — essentially the whole demand list from Lesson 2, with links. Module 5 turns this work into a CV, a LinkedIn, and a story that gets you hired.

prompts: Review my capstone spec: [PASTE ARCHITECTURE]. Act as a hiring engineer: what's missing, what's overbuilt, and what one addition would most increase its interview value?

Design memory extraction for a personal assistant: what fact types to store (preferences, people, projects, commitments), the Pydantic schema, when to run extraction, and how to keep the injected summary under 150 tokens.
Write my 3-minute capstone demo script: conversation → memory recall → tool use → MCP connection. Include exact example lines the agent should say, and transitions for a non-technical viewer.
