Submit per Lesson 24's checklist. Then take an evening off — you've built four deployed AI systems, and that puts you ahead of most applicants for every job you're about to apply to.

lessons.title: The CV That Passes AI Screeners (ATS Keywords)
lessons.goal: Write a CV engineered for both machines and humans — the exact ATS keywords recruiters search, quantified project bullets, and a format that survives any parser.
lessons.audio_intro: Harsh truth: before any human sees your CV, software reads it. Recruiters search their database by keywords, and in the 2026 AI market those keywords are known: Python, RAG, LangChain, LangGraph, MCP, agents, vector databases, evals, prompt engineering. Miss them and you're invisible; stuff them without evidence and you're noise. Today we build a CV both honest and findable: clean, parser-proof structure, the exact vocabulary recruiters search, and bullets that quantify shipped work — you now have shipped work to quantify. Let's write one that gets you called.

sections.body: Applicant tracking systems parse your CV into fields, and recruiters **search by keyword**: 'show me Python AND RAG, junior, open to hybrid.' The keywords that matter in the current agentic market map directly to the demand list from Lesson 2 — Python, RAG, LangChain, LangGraph, MCP, agents, vector database, evals, prompt engineering, Docker, CI/CD, FastAPI, Kubernetes. Rules that keep you parseable: one column, no text in images, no exotic fonts, standard section headers ('Experience', 'Projects', 'Skills'), and a `.docx` or clean PDF. Test it: paste your CV into any free ATS checker, or into an LLM with the prompt 'extract my skills from this CV' — what comes out is what recruiters can find.

A skills list alone proves nothing. The pattern that works: **keyword + artifact + number**:

- 'Built and deployed a customer-support agent (LangGraph, RAG over 50-doc knowledge base, Docker, FastAPI) — 30-case eval suite in CI, 88% answer faithfulness; public demo.'
- 'Implemented MCP server exposing 4 tools; integrated with external agent clients.'
- 'Reduced LLM batch-processing cost 60% by switching classification to mini model with structured outputs.'

Every line is a claim a recruiter can click — your four deployed repos are the receipts. This is why the course made you ship: the CV almost writes itself. One page, projects above education if the projects are stronger — and yours are.

The layout that survives parsing and impresses humans:

- **Header**: name, location, LinkedIn, GitHub, portfolio site.
- **Summary, 3 lines**: 'Junior software engineer specializing in AI applications. Shipped four deployed LLM systems: agents (LangGraph), RAG, MCP tools, with eval suites and CI. Python, FastAPI, Docker.'
- **Projects** (the star section): your four, each 2–3 evidence bullets with links.
- **Experience**: any work history, reframed for AI relevance — automated a report, built a script, saved hours.
- **Skills**: the keyword block, grouped (Languages / AI & Agents / Infra).
- **Education & certificates**: BINA certificate, date, capstone link.

For career-changers: projects ARE your experience. Lead with them, unapologetically.

Send a slightly different CV per application — it doubles response rates. The 15-minute routine: paste the job posting into an LLM with your CV and ask: 'List every required keyword missing from my CV, and rewrite my three most relevant bullets to mirror this posting's language — without inventing anything.' Then sanity-check every claim: the LLM embellishes, and you don't lie on a CV — keywords must reflect work you actually did, because Lessons 22–23 will interrogate it. Keep a master CV; generate tailored copies per posting in `/cvs`. Recruiters search exactly the words in their posting — mirroring their language is fair play; fabricating is career suicide.

prompts: Here is my CV: [PASTE]. Here is a job posting: [PASTE]. List every keyword the posting wants that my CV lacks, then rewrite my 3 most relevant bullets to mirror the posting — keep every claim true to my actual work.

Act as an ATS parser: extract every skill, tool, and job title from my CV [PASTE] into a flat list. Then tell me which of these are missing: Python, RAG, LangChain, LangGraph, MCP, agents, vector database, evals, prompt engineering, Docker, FastAPI.
Rewrite these project bullets to be quantified and ATS-friendly without inventing facts: [PASTE YOUR BULLETS]. Keep keyword + artifact + number structure.
lessons.exercise: Produce your master CV: one page, projects-first, four deployed artifacts with links, the full keyword set from this lesson, zero unverifiable claims. Run it through an ATS parser or LLM extraction test and fix what's missing. Save the master and one tailored version for a real posting you saved in Lesson 2. Module 5 continues with LinkedIn next.

lessons.title: LinkedIn Optimization for AI Careers
lessons.goal: Turn LinkedIn into an inbound channel — headline, About section, and activity that surface you to recruiters searching for the exact AI skills you now have.
lessons.audio_intro: Recruiters don't wait for your application — they search LinkedIn the way they search CV databases: by keyword. In this lesson we optimize your profile so search finds you: a headline that reads like the job you want, an About section that tells your shipped-projects story in the first two lines, skills set to the exact terms from the market index, and a light posting rhythm that signals you're active in the field. LinkedIn is a search engine — SEO for your career. Let's get you found.

sections.body: The headline follows you everywhere and is heavily weighted in recruiter search. Bad: 'Aspiring AI enthusiast.' Good: **'AI Engineer | Python, LangGraph, RAG, MCP | Built & deployed 4 agent systems — demos in Featured'**. Formula: target role + core keywords + proof hook. Fill the rest of the profile skeleton the same way: your headline, About, experience titles, and skills field are all searchable — the skills section especially, since recruiters filter by exact skills. Load every true one: Python, LangChain, LangGraph, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), MCP, vector databases, FastAPI, Docker, prompt engineering, LLM evaluation. Each is a door recruiters can find you through.

sections.h: About: the first two lines are everything
sections.body: Nobody clicks 'see more' without a reason, so the first two lines must carry the story: 'I build and deploy AI agents — support agents, document analyzers, multi-agent pipelines. Four shipped systems, each with public demos and eval suites.' Then the About earns trust with specifics: the four projects in one line each, with links; the tools; a sentence on how you work (shipped > perfect, measured > guessed); and a clear call to action ('Open to junior AI/software engineering roles — reach me here'). Write it in first person, plain, confident. Then pin your best repo and demo video in the **Featured** section — profile visitors are one click from proof of your work.

A profile gets you found; activity gets you remembered. Sustainable rhythm, 30 minutes a week:

- **One post a week** documenting what you build: a screenshot, what it does, one thing you learned. 'Built an MCP server for my assistant — one tool, 20 lines, now any agent client can use it.' Build-in-public posts from your Module 4 work are endless material.
- **Comment daily** on posts by AI engineers and companies you'd work for — substantive comments, not 'Great post!'
- **Follow** the employers from Lesson 2 (Salesforce, Databricks, OpenAI, Palantir, Citi, Cisco, Anthropic) and their engineering leads.

Recruiters check activity before reaching out. A profile with three months of build-in-public posts reads as 'actively becoming an engineer' — which is precisely what you are.

Practical switches: set 'Open to Work' for the titles you want (recruiter-only visibility if you're employed); turn on 'Signal your interest' to recruiters at target companies; list the BINA certificate in Licenses & Certifications; and use a photo + banner — a simple code-editor screenshot banner beats a default gradient. Networking, uncreepily: when you connect, one personalized line referencing their work, not a job ask. Engage with your cohort's posts — reciprocity is real. And keep your CV's claims and your LinkedIn claims identical: recruiters cross-check, and consistency reads as honesty. Lesson 19 arms the messages you'll send.

prompts: Write 3 LinkedIn headline options for me: target role 'AI / junior software engineer (AI applications)', keywords Python, LangGraph, RAG, MCP, agents. Under 220 characters each, no buzzword soup. My background: [SUMMARIZE].

Draft my LinkedIn About section, first person: four deployed AI projects (support agent, document analyzer, multi-agent pipeline, assistant with MCP), build-in-public style, clear 'open to work' CTA. 150-200 words, plain and confident.
Turn this week's project work into a build-in-public LinkedIn post: [PASTE NOTES]. Hook in the first line, one visual suggestion, one lesson learned, under 150 words, no hashtags beyond 3.
lessons.exercise: Optimize your LinkedIn end-to-end: new headline, About with Featured links, full skills list, open-to-work settings, BINA certificate listed. Post your first build-in-public item (screenshot + 4 sentences about a Module 4 project). Then comment substantively on two posts from people at your target companies. Check your profile in an incognito window — would a recruiter searching 'LangGraph' find you?

lessons.title: Cover Letters That Don't Suck
lessons.goal: Write short, specific cover letters that get read — a repeatable formula built on the company's actual problem, your shipped proof, and zero clichés.
lessons.audio_intro: Most cover letters are terrible because they're about the applicant. The ones that work are about the employer's problem — and how your shipped projects attack it. In this lesson: a tight formula for letters that get read in twenty seconds, the research step most people skip, and how to use your four deployed systems as evidence no other junior can match. Plus the adaptation trick — one master letter, five minutes per application — and the short-message versions for LinkedIn and email. Let's write.

sections.body: Symptoms of the dead letter: 'I am writing to express my interest…' · 'I am a highly motivated self-starter…' · 'I believe my skills would be a great fit…' — all about you, none about them, nothing checkable. The reader (a hiring manager with 40 letters and 6 minutes) is asking exactly one question: *can this person do the specific thing we need, and is it worth 30 minutes to find out?* A good letter answers it in the first three lines with a concrete claim plus a link. Your unfair advantage after Module 4: most juniors write 'passionate about AI'; you write 'here are four deployed systems — try one.'

Five short paragraphs, 150–200 words total:

1. **The hook — their problem, in their words.** From the posting and 10 minutes of research: 'You're hiring an engineer to scale [Company]'s support automation beyond scripted flows.'
2. **The claim.** 'I build and deploy exactly those systems: four shipped LLM projects — agents, RAG, MCP tools — each with public demos.'
3. **The proof, one best match.** Two sentences on the project that maps to their need, with the link and a number: '30-case eval suite, 88% faithfulness.'
4. **The specifics.** Their stack where it overlaps yours: LangGraph, RAG, FastAPI, Docker.
5. **The ask.** 'Happy to walk through the demo in 15 minutes.'

No 'to whom it may concern' — find a name on LinkedIn. Attach nothing; link everything.

sections.h: Research: the 10 minutes that double callbacks
sections.body: Before writing, answer three questions: **What does this company actually build or automate?** (product pages, engineering blog, recent launches.) **What does the posting repeat?** — words appearing three or more times are the real job. **Who reads it?** — a recruiter screens for keywords, an engineering manager for judgment, so include one of each: the keyword line ('Python, LangGraph, RAG') and a judgment line ('chose evals-in-CI over chasing a bigger model because measured beats guessed'). If the company is Israeli or US-based, note the language norms — direct, specific, no formality theater. Ten minutes of research shows up as specificity, and specificity reads as competence.

sections.h: The master letter and the short versions
sections.body: Write one master letter for your top target role, then adapt per application by swapping paragraphs 1, 3, and 4 — five minutes each, keep a `/letters` folder with one file per company so you can track what you sent. For LinkedIn messages and email intros, compress the formula to three sentences: hook on their problem → your claim + best link → the ask. Example: 'Saw you're scaling agentic support at [Company] — I've shipped a deployed LangGraph support agent with evals (link). Worth 15 minutes?' Same spine, shorter bones. Never send a letter a model wrote unedited — recruiters can smell a template, and one hallucinated claim about their company ends the conversation.

prompts: Here is a job posting [PASTE] and my projects [PASTE SUMMARY]. Write a cover letter using: hook about their problem → my claim → one best project with link → stack overlap → 15-minute ask. Under 180 words, no clichés. Then list the 3 ways it's tailored, so I can verify each.
Compress my cover letter [PASTE] into a 3-sentence LinkedIn message to a hiring manager, first line about their problem, last line a low-pressure ask.
Review this cover letter like a busy hiring manager with 40 to read: [PASTE]. Cut it to under 150 words, flag any cliché or unverifiable claim, and score it 1-10 for specificity.
lessons.exercise: Write your master cover letter for a real posting from your Lesson 2 target list, plus one tailored variant for a second posting. Run both through the cliché-and-claims review prompt, verify every claim maps to real work, and send the master to one real application this week — momentum beats perfection. File both in `/letters`.

lessons.title: GitHub Portfolio Polish (README, Demo Links)
lessons.goal: Turn your four project repos into a recruiter-ready portfolio — profile README, pinned repos, consistent quality bar, and demo links that work when clicked at 2am.
lessons.audio_intro: Your GitHub is the only part of your application an engineer will definitely open — and many recruiters open it before the CV's second page. In this lesson we polish it like a product: a profile README that routes visitors to your best work, four pinned repos that each pass the thirty-second scan — clear hook, live link, screenshot, eval numbers — and a quality pass that removes the embarrassing stuff. The goal: any stranger landing on your profile sees in half a minute that you ship real AI systems.

sections.body: github.com/you is a landing page — treat it like one. Create a **profile README** (a repo named exactly like your username): two lines on who you are ('AI engineer — I build and deploy agents, RAG systems, and MCP tools'), the four projects as a linked list with one-line descriptions, stack keywords in compact badges, and links to LinkedIn and your demo video. Then **pin** the four project repos (not your practice repos). Set your contribution graph visible — a few months of consistent commits is quiet proof of momentum. Check everything in an incognito window: what a stranger sees in 30 seconds is the only thing that counts.

Each project repo must pass this checklist, no exceptions:

- **Hook line**: 'Customer-support agent: classifies, retrieves, answers with citations, human-gated refunds — deployed.'
- **Live demo link at the top** — tested this week, and a screenshot or GIF right below it (links die; screenshots don't).
- **Quickstart that actually runs**: `cp .env.example .env`, `docker compose up`, done.
- **Architecture note**: 4–6 lines or a simple diagram — FastAPI → LangGraph → Chroma → evals in CI.
- **Eval table** in the README with dates.
- **License** file (MIT).

The polish pass: archive or make private the tutorial repos, fix the broken READMEs you'd be embarrassed by, and remove any file named `final_v2_REAL.py`. Your history is fine — messy *front doors* are not.

A recruiter clicking your link at 2am must see something working. Free-tier apps sleep — so: add a warm-up or a fast cold start, a friendly loading state, and a **static fallback**: a pre-run demo page or recording for when the live demo hiccups ('Live demo — if it's sleeping, watch the 90-second video'). Keep two sample datasets pre-loaded in every app (Lesson 14 rule) so no link ever shows an empty screen. Then monitor: put a `/health` check on a free uptime monitor so you get an email before a recruiter gets an error page. 'Deployed and maintained' is the whole message — the difference between a portfolio and a graveyard is whether the links work six months later, and interviews are exactly when you find out.

One page that ties it together — GitHub Pages is free: your one-liner, the four projects with screenshots and live links, the demo video, and contact. Design bar: clean and readable, not fancy — dark-mode-friendly, mobile-friendly, no frameworks needed. If you built the multi-agent content pipeline (Lesson 15), let it write your first drafts — dogfooding your own AI system is itself a talking point. Cross-link everything: site → repos → LinkedIn → CV. When Module 6's applications ask for 'portfolio URL,' this is the link you give. One hour of assembly, permanent professional presence.

prompts: Review my GitHub profile like a hiring engineer with 30 seconds: [PASTE PROFILE README + LIST OF REPOS]. Score it, list what's confusing, and give me the 5 highest-impact fixes.

Write hook lines (one sentence each) for my four project repos: support agent, document analyzer, multi-agent pipeline, personal assistant with MCP. Make each concrete with one number or capability — no adjectives.

Create a README quality checklist I can run against any repo, in table form, with pass/fail criteria: hook, demo link, screenshot, quickstart, architecture, evals, license. Then apply it to [PASTE MY README] and report gaps.
lessons.exercise: Do the full polish pass: profile README, four pinned repos upgraded to the quality bar, all demo links tested (fix or add fallbacks), messy repos archived, and optionally the portfolio site. Then send your GitHub URL to one person outside tech and ask what they think you do — if they can't tell, fix the top of the profile. Module 6 starts the actual hunt.

lessons.title: Where the Jobs Actually Are: Titles, Employers, Salary, Negotiation
lessons.goal: Run the job hunt like a sales pipeline — search the right titles and employers, know realistic salary bands, and negotiate the first offer without losing it.
lessons.audio_intro: Module 6 — the hunt. Today, the terrain: where the jobs actually are. We'll search like recruiters think — by title families and keyword sets, not by scrolling. We'll name the employer categories actually hiring for agentic AI, from forward-deployed leaders like Salesforce, Databricks, OpenAI, Palantir, Citi, Cisco, and Anthropic to the thousands of regular companies adopting AI. We'll set realistic salary expectations, because guessing wrong costs you money in both directions. And we'll cover negotiation, including the counteroffer script that usually works. Strategy beats volume. Let's hunt smart.

sections.body: Job boards rank and filter by keyword, so search keyword families, not titles: **'Python RAG'**, **'LangGraph'**, **'LangChain'**, **'MCP'**, **'AI agent developer'**, **'LLM application'**, plus the adjacent-entry titles from Lesson 2: junior software engineer (AI), automation engineer, data analyst/engineer, solutions engineer, forward-deployed engineer (junior variants exist — search it directly). Set alerts for five searches on LinkedIn, and add the aggregators for AI-specific boards. Then go around the boards: companies adopting AI list 'AI' in their engineering blogs — a 'careers' page check on 20 such companies beats 200 cold applications. Track everything in a spreadsheet: company, role, date, contact, status, next step.

Four employer buckets, in order of realistic entry:

1. **AI-native companies** — Salesforce, Databricks, OpenAI, Palantir, Citi, Cisco, Anthropic and their peers are competing hardest for agentic talent (they anchor the forward-deployed engineer wave). Junior roles are scarce but solutions/engineering-support paths exist.
2. **Enterprises adopting AI** — banks, insurers, retail, healthcare: thousands of internal AI-application and automation roles. The realistic entry door, and RAG/agents experience maps perfectly.
3. **Startups and agencies** — fast, title-flexible, proof-over-credentials; your deployed portfolio is exactly their hiring test.
4. **In-house translation** — your current employer: proposing an AI feature where you already work is often the single fastest path into AI work.

In Israel, add the local angle: a dense startup ecosystem plus multinationals, many hiring for exactly this stack. Local meetups and LinkedIn groups are disproportionately effective there.

sections.h: Salary: know the band before they ask
sections.body: Research before numbers: check levels-style sites, LinkedIn salary insights, and — most reliably — ask three people in your market what junior AI-application roles pay; local Facebook/WhatsApp groups and peer networks beat any aggregator. For orientation only: US junior-to-mid AI/software engineering roles commonly span roughly the low-to-mid $100Ks, with total comp higher at AI-native companies; Israeli junior AI/software roles commonly span roughly ₪20K–₪35K monthly depending on seniority-adjacent skills. Treat these as starting points to verify locally — bands move fast, and your deployed portfolio pushes you toward the top of any junior band. When asked for expectations, answer with a researched range and anchor to evidence: 'Based on my research, X to Y — I'm flexible on structure.'

Rules that keep offers alive: **never negotiate before intent** — first get the offer in writing. **Negotiate the band, not a demand**: 'Based on my research for this scope, I was expecting closer to X — is there flexibility?' **Negotiate one thing primarily** (base), but know the other levers: sign-on, start date, education budget, hybrid days. **Silence is a tool** — after their counter, 'let me think about it overnight' is professional, not rude. And the fallback: if the number won't move, ask for a 6-month review with agreed criteria — 'If I ship X by then, we revisit.' That converts a no into a milestone, and you will ship X. You have receipts for your worth now; use them calmly.

prompts: I'm targeting junior AI-application roles in [YOUR MARKET: e.g., Tel Aviv / US remote]. Build me a 10-search alert strategy: exact search strings, which boards, and how to find the 30% of postings never posted to big boards.

A recruiter asked my salary expectations for a junior AI/software role. Script me: (1) a deflecting first answer, (2) a researched-range answer with my evidence, (3) a polite response if they push for one number. My situation: [SUMMARIZE].
I have an offer: [PASTE DETAILS]. Walk me through deciding: how to compare total comp, what to negotiate first, exact phrasing for the ask, and what not to do.
lessons.exercise: Set up your hunt infrastructure: 5 saved job alerts with the keyword families from this lesson, a tracking spreadsheet with 10 real target companies (include at least 3 from your Lesson 2 list), salary research for your market written down as a range with sources, and a one-page negotiation script saved to `/career`. Apply to two roles this week — tailored CV, letter from Lesson 19, portfolio link in the first line of the application.

lessons.title: Interview Prep with an AI Interviewer
lessons.goal: Prepare for both technical and behavioral AI-engineering interviews — using an AI interviewer to drill answers — with the question set you'll actually face and stories that prove you ship.
lessons.audio_intro: Interviews for AI roles have a predictable shape — and you have an unfair advantage: a tireless interviewer living in your browser. In this lesson we set up AI-driven mock interviews: technical drills on your own projects — 'walk me through your RAG design; why that chunk size; how do you know it works?' — and behavioral rounds using the STAR format. We'll cover the ten likeliest questions, answers backed by your four deployed projects, and the anti-patterns that sink juniors: vagueness, buzzwords, perfection claims. Let's drill.

sections.body: AI-application interviews typically run: (1) a recruiter screen for keywords and salary band; (2) a technical conversation — your projects, live coding in Python, and design questions ('how would you build a support agent for X?'); (3) sometimes a take-home (Lesson 23); (4) a behavioral round. The technical rounds lean hard on **your own repos** — this favors you enormously: you'll be asked about code you wrote, shipped, and evaluated. Question set to prepare: explain RAG end-to-end; agents vs. workflows and when each fits; what MCP is and why it exists; how you prevent hallucinations; how you'd evaluate an agent you didn't build; your eval methodology; cost/latency trade-offs. Every one is a Lesson 9–12 topic — you have real answers.

Set up a drill loop with a chatbot — this is the prompt to save:

> 'You are a senior AI engineer interviewing me for a junior AI-application role. One question at a time; wait for my answer. Alternate technical questions about my projects (ask follow-ups like a real interviewer — challenge my design choices) and behavioral questions. After 8 questions, stop and give me a brutally honest scorecard: three things that sounded strong, three that sounded weak or vague, and the exact wording I should have used.'

Run it 2–3 times a week, on voice where possible. Push paste your actual READMEs and code so the drill targets your real work. Vary the persona: friendly recruiter, skeptical staff engineer, non-technical founder. Nerves fade with repetition — this is a flight simulator for conversations that decide salaries.

sections.h: STAR stories from your own history
sections.body:
Behavioral rounds need five prepared stories, and Module 4 gave you every one:

1. **Shipped under constraints** — the support agent built layer-by-layer with evals ('deadline pressure, prioritized the human-gate and evals over extra features').
2. **Debugged something hard** — the RAG retrieval you fixed with the bad-answer diagnosis from Lesson 9.
3. **Made a trade-off** — mini model vs. frontier model with the cost numbers.
4. **Learned fast** — MCP from zero to a working server in a week.
5. **Disagreed / took feedback** — any code review you took from the AI interviewer or a peer, then improved.

Format each as **STAR** — Situation, Task, Action, Result — 60–90 seconds spoken, out loud, timed. Practice with your AI interviewer until each story lands under two minutes with a number at the end.

What kills otherwise-passable candidates: **vagueness** ('it worked pretty well') — always attach a number; **buzzwords without proof** — saying 'MCP' earns a follow-up question, and you can answer it, so no problem — but never name-drop what you can't whiteboard; **claiming solo perfection** — say instead 'my first version had a routing bug; here's how I found it with traces,' because engineers trust people who find their own bugs; **trashing your projects** — confidence with evidence, not apology; **not asking questions back** — prepare three ('how do you eval changes here? what does the agent stack look like? what does success look like in 90 days?'). Questions that assume production reality mark you as someone who's shipped — because you have.

prompts: Be my AI interviewer: senior engineer, junior AI-application role, one question at a time. Alternate technical questions about my projects (READMEs: [PASTE]) and behavioral STAR questions; challenge weak answers with follow-ups. After 8 questions, give me a scorecard: 3 strengths, 3 weaknesses, better wording for my worst answer.

Here are the 10 questions I'm most likely to face in [TARGET ROLE]. For each, give me: what the interviewer is really testing, a strong 60-second answer structure, and the follow-up trap question. My projects: [SUMMARIZE].
Rewrite my STAR story to be tighter and end with a number: [PASTE STORY]. Keep it under 90 seconds spoken, first person, no jargon unless it earns its place.
lessons.exercise: Complete three full mock interviews with your AI interviewer this week (one recruiter persona, one skeptical engineer, one founder). After each, write down your weakest answer and drill it twice more. Prepare and rehearse your five STAR stories out loud, timed. Record yourself once — watch it once — then never again. You'll be more rehearsed than almost every competing junior candidate.

lessons.title: Take-Home Assignments: Build a RAG or Agent Under Time Pressure
lessons.goal: Master the AI-engineering take-home — scope ruthlessly, build a working RAG or agent in hours not days, and submit with the README and trade-off notes that get you hired.
lessons.audio_intro: The take-home is where AI-engineering interviews get real: 'Build a small RAG or agent over this dataset — you have three days.' Most candidates fail it the same way: over-building, late submission, no evaluation. You won't. In this lesson: how to scope a take-home to the rubric, a time-boxed plan that always ends with something working, the two files reviewers read first, and presenting trade-offs as strengths. We'll also simulate the pressure with a timed mini take-home. Your last gate before offers. Let's make it routine.

sections.body: A take-home rubric usually has four silent criteria: **does it work** (they will run it — a broken submission with great ideas scores below a working one with rough edges); **is the code sane** (small functions, error handling, no 400-line notebook exported as an app); **did you make sensible trade-offs** (documented choices beat hidden perfection); **can I work with this person** (README tone, commit hygiene). What loses points: frameworks you can't explain, no tests, no error handling on API calls, hardcoded keys, and — the classic — spending the whole budget on polish for one path while the main flow breaks on edge cases. Scope to the rubric: working end-to-end first, extras only if time remains.

For a typical 'small RAG/agent, few days' assignment:

- **Hour 0 — read and scope.** Extract explicit requirements into a checklist; identify the core loop and mark everything else 'nice to have.' Write the plan at the top of your README.
- **Hours 1–3 — walking skeleton.** Data in → model call → answer out, deployed or runnable via one command. Ugly is fine; working is everything.
- **Hours 4–8 — quality pass.** Pydantic outputs, retry on API calls, top-k retrieval with citations, a `/health` route. Reuse your Module 3 patterns — you've built this before.
- **Hour 9 — evals, minimum viable.** 10 golden questions, pass rate printed. A take-home *with* an eval loop beats most of the pool.
- **Final hour — README and demo.**

Stop when the plan says stop. Over-building reads as poor judgment, not dedication.

sections.h: The two files that decide it
sections.body: Reviewers open two files first: the **README** and your **main module**. README structure that wins: one-line description; 30-second quickstart (`docker compose up`); a short 'decisions & trade-offs' section — 'chunked on section headers at ~400 tokens because the docs have strong structure; used Chroma for zero-config local dev; single mini-model for cost; evals: 10 cases, 80% faithful (failures concentrated in table-heavy pages — noted, not fixed, for scope)' — that paragraph is where seniors are made. Then 'what I'd do with more time,' honestly, 3 items. The main module should read like the README promised: clean names, typed functions, `try/except` around anything that touches the network. And run `gitleaks` before pushing — a committed key in a take-home is an automatic fail at too many companies.

sections.h: Presenting it and the follow-up call
sections.body: After submission comes the review call — prepare like Lesson 22's drill: a 3-minute walkthrough (problem → design → demo → evals), and answers for the questions your README invites: 'why that chunk size?' 'how would this scale?' 'what broke?' Know your own numbers cold (eval pass rate, cost per query, latency) and volunteer one limitation before they find it — 'table extraction is the weak spot; I'd add a table-aware parser' — because finding your own bugs is exactly the senior signal they're grading. If the assignment demands more than ~8–10 hours for a junior role without pay, it's fair to ask about scope — companies that respect candidates respect the question.

prompts: Here is my take-home assignment: [PASTE BRIEF]. Extract the explicit requirements as a checklist, identify the core loop, and propose a time-boxed plan for [HOURS] hours — including what I will deliberately NOT build. Flag any requirement that is ambiguous enough to ask about.
Write the 'decisions & trade-offs' section of my take-home README from these notes: [PASTE YOUR CHOICES]. Honest engineer voice, one short paragraph plus a 'with more time' list of 3 items.
I finished my take-home (RAG over [DATASET], evals at [SCORE]). Give me the 10 hardest follow-up questions the reviewer will ask on the call, with strong 30-second answers grounded in my actual work.

Follow the time-boxed plan exactly, push to GitHub, then have your Lesson 22 AI interviewer grill you on it. Not only is it practice — the repo itself becomes portfolio artifact five.

lessons.title: Certificate Exam Prep + Final Project Submission
lessons.goal: Consolidate everything for the BINA certificate exam and final submission — the knowledge check covering all 24 lessons, the project package checklist, and the career sprint that starts the day after.
lessons.audio_intro: Final lesson — but really, a launch. Today we prepare three things: the BINA certificate exam, your capstone submission, and the sprint that starts the moment you pass. We'll review the whole arc — LLMs, Python, structured outputs, RAG, deployment, agents, MCP, evals, marketing, interviewing — as a checklist, not a cram, because the exam tests the judgment you've built for twenty-four lessons. Then the submission package, and your first thirty days after certification, planned like a project. A certificate without applications is just paper. Let's close strong.

sections.h: The exam: what it covers and how to review
sections.body: The certificate exam checks working understanding, not memorization. Areas, mapped to modules: LLM fundamentals — tokens, context, hallucinations, grounding (Lessons 1, 3–4); Python and API practice — schemas, retries, cost control (5–7); RAG — chunking, embeddings, vector search, citations (9); deployment — FastAPI, Docker, CI (10); agents — function calling, LangGraph, MCP, safety gates (11); evals — golden sets, LLM-as-judge, traces (12); career — market data, ATS keywords, interview structure (2, 17, 22). Review method: for each area, explain it out loud in 60 seconds without notes — the same fluency the interviewers will test. Where you stall, re-read that lesson's sections and re-run its exercise. Your projects are your notes: every concept is something you shipped.

Final submission checklist — everything due together:

- **Capstone repo**: assistant agent with memory, tools, MCP server — passing CI with evals.
- **Deployed URL**: live and health-checked (Lesson 20's uptime monitor running).
- **Demo video**: the 3-minute walkthrough from Lesson 16.
- **Design-decisions doc**: one page, what you chose and rejected, and why.
- **Portfolio set**: all four project repos passing the Lesson 20 quality bar, pinned, with the profile README.
- **Career assets**: master CV, LinkedIn optimized, one application already sent (Lesson 21's exercise).

Verify like an engineer would: run every link from an incognito browser, run `gitleaks`, re-run the CI suites. If the package passes your own review, it passes ours.

Look at what you can put on a CV, with links: Python, structured LLM outputs, RAG built from scratch, FastAPI + Docker + CI deployment, LangGraph agents, LangChain, function calling, MCP servers, evals and observability — mapped almost one-to-one onto the 2026 demand list: Python (50% of agentic postings), cloud (34%), MCP (27%), RAG (26%), LangChain (15%), LangGraph (13%), vector DBs (13%), tool use (11%), evals (9%). Four deployed systems with public URLs — when only ~4% of AI-engineer postings are entry-level, shipped proof is exactly how you compete. And the working habits — test it, measure it, cite it, ship it — are the ones employers keep. That combination is your credential; the certificate just makes it official.

Passing the exam is a milestone, not a finish line. Run the next 30 days like a project:

- **Week 1**: five tailored applications to Lesson 2 target companies; share the capstone demo on LinkedIn; tell your network you're looking.
- **Week 2**: five more applications plus direct outreach — three short messages (Lesson 19 formula) to engineers at target companies; keep one build-in-public post a week.
- **Week 3**: keep the AI-interviewer drills at twice a week until offers arrive; do one timed take-home simulation if any are pending.
- **Week 4**: iterate on feedback — track which applications convert, fix your weakest interview answer, and consider the internal-transfer path (Lesson 21, bucket 4).

Treat 'land the role' exactly like your capstone: scope it, measure it, ship it.
